  "text": "By morning Tobias had worn a pale place in the brim of his cap.

He had sat in the church all night, holding it between his knees. When the woman came to sweep, he lifted his feet. She swept beneath them. Neither asked the other anything.

Outside, the village had begun its ordinary work. A cart went past with an empty fish box rattling in the bed. Tobias waited until it had turned the corner before he took the beach road.

From the bend he could see Maren's house. The door was shut. The front window held the dull square of the sky.

He went as far as the first post.

There were eleven. He counted them twice, keeping his finger against the seam of his coat. At the porch, the last stood a little crooked. He remembered her father setting it, refusing help, kneeling to pack the earth with the heel of his hand.

Tobias had brought bread. He had not known until then what he meant to do with it.

He climbed the path and put the loaf on the step. The paper crackled loudly. He tucked its loose edge underneath so it would not blow away.

Through the window he saw the lamp, unlit, on the sill. Beyond it lay the rug.

He raised his hand to knock.

Under the door, very slowly, the edge of the bread paper drew inward and stopped.

Tobias lowered his hand. He left the loaf where it was.",

  "text": "At the bottom of the path Tobias found flour on his sleeve.

He brushed it off. Then he stood with his hand against the post, looking down the road toward the village.

The baker would be opening his shutters. There would be somewhere to sit, and a stove, and questions that could be answered by saying he had not slept.

He went the other way.

On the beach the tide had left a length of rope among the weed. Tobias bent to free it, working patiently at a knot that held nothing. He had almost loosened it when he heard the door.

Not a slam. Only the sound of wood catching against a swollen frame.

He straightened. From here the bank concealed the house except for its chimney. No smoke came from it.

He waited with the rope in his hands.

Once, in winter, Maren had called down to him from that bank. She had wanted him to look at something she was carrying in her apron. He remembered climbing toward her, annoyed at leaving his work. What she had shown him was gone from his memory. He could recall only her hands gathering the cloth.

The knot came loose.

Tobias laid the rope above the tide line, coiled so someone might use it.

When he returned to the road, the loaf was still on the step. The paper had been folded neatly over it.

Beside it stood a cup.

He knew the cup. He could have named the cupboard where it belonged.

He climbed the path again.",

  "text": "The cup was empty. A little sand lay in the bottom, though the step was clean.

Tobias lifted it by the handle. There was the chip beneath his thumb. He had made it years ago, knocking the cup against the pump, and had put it back with the damaged side toward the wall.

Maren had turned it around each morning.

He set it down.

Through the door he could hear something being dragged, a short distance at a time. He thought of the kitchen chair with its uneven legs. To move it quietly you had to lift it. He had told her that often enough.

The sound stopped.

‘I brought enough for two,’ he said.

He had not meant to say it. The loaf was small, and yesterday he had eaten nothing.

Somewhere inside, a spoon touched the rim of a bowl.

Tobias sat on the step. He unfolded the paper and broke the bread, catching the crumbs in his palm. One half he placed beside the cup. The other he kept on his knee.

The sun had reached the road below. A cart went past, its driver walking beside the horse. Tobias lowered his head until the wheels could no longer be heard.

Then he ate the crumbs.

Behind him, the latch rose. The door pressed against his coat and stopped.

He could have stood. Instead he leaned forward just enough to let it open.

A familiar smell came through the gap: damp wool, cold ashes, the apples stored beneath the stairs.

He moved his half of the bread off his knee.",
